0.

E'OREb'ORD

0.1 This Indian Standard

was adopted by the Indian Standards Institution on 15 June 1983, after the draft finalized by the Chemical Standards Sectional Committee lrad been approved by the Chemical Division Council.

0.2 This standard was first published in 1962 covering only modified Newer techniques for determination of arsenic had Gutzeit method. and one such method was based on silver been increasingly applied, diethyldithiocarbamate. The standard was revised in 1971 to incorporate this method. This method assists in determining the actual arsenic content as against the limit test provided by modified Gutzeit method. Selection ofeither silver diethyldithiocarbamate or modified Gutzeit method has to be judged from the end use. 0.3 The second revision of the standard has been undertaken to align it with ISO 2590-1973 `General method for the determination of arsenicSilver diethyldithiocarbamate photometric method', issued by the InterAssistance has also been national Organization for Standardization. derived from the Dot : 47jl N. 62 `General method for the diethyldithiocarbamate photometric method', issued by the International Organization for Standardization. 0.4 Before the test can be applied to the material, any arsenic present has to be quantitatively converted into its simple derivatives like arsenic trichloride or pentachloride which can be completely reduced to arsine by action of zinc in presence of dilute acid. These derivatives should be free from interfering substances like nitrate, copper, silver, mercury, cobalt, nickel, molybdenum and palladium which are to be removed suitably and taken in the desired volume containing the desired amount of free acid. Though the preparation of test solutton shall be dealt by individual material specifications, the possible treatments either alone or Such treatments are in combination, will be suitable for most samples. prescribed in Appendix A for guidance. 3

IS:2088-1983
0.5 In reporting the result of a test or analysis made in accordance with this standard, if the final value, observed or calculated, is to be rounded off, it shall be done in accordance with IS : 2-1960*.

prescribes methods for determination of arsenic,

5. PROCEDURE

5.1 Modified Gutzeit Method - Prepare the solution of the material as specified in the individual material specification ( SL'C also Appendix A). Place the dry lead acetate paper in the lower portion of the tube B and cotton ,vool moistened with lead acetate in its upper portion. Place the bl-omide paper in tube A and connect the sensitized strip of mercuric Into-oc:uce the solution .of the tubes together with a rubber stopper. material into the bottle C and add 10 ml of tlilute sulphuric arid. Add 0.5 ml ofstannous chloride solution, 5 ml of potassium iodide solution and make up the volume with water to about 50 ml. Mix the contents Fit in position the rubber stopper and drop in about 10 6 of zinc. the tube B Immediately. Place the bottle in a warm place at carryinp about 40�C. Remove the test strips after 40 minutes with the help of tweezers. Conduct the test in exactly similar manner by using a volume of standard arsenic solution as specified in the material specification, in of the material and compare the stain produced place of the solution with the material with that produced with the arsenic solution.
*Specification tspecification for rcctificd spirit ( revised ). for ether ( revLed ).

IS : 2088 - 1983 5.1.1 The limit prescribed in the material specification shall be taken as not having been exceeded if the length of the stain as well as the intensity of its colour produced in the test with the material is not greater than those produced with the corresponding standard arsenic solution. 5.2 Silver Diethyldithiocarbamate Method in a solution of silver diethyldithio-

5.2.2 Evolution of Arsine - Transfer to a series of 100 ml conical flasks, aliquots of standard arsenic solution corresponding to 0, 5, 10, 15, 20 and 25 tug of arsenic and `proceed as given in 5.2.2.1. 5.2.2.1 Add 10 ml of concentrated hydrochloric acid and dilute to 50 -+ 5 ml wit11 water. Add 2 ml of potassium iodide and stannous chloride solution respectively. Mix well and let it stand for 15 to 20 Pack lightly the top third of the connecting tube with minutes. impregnated absorbent cotton wool and assemble an the absorption Transfer 5.0 ml of silver diethyldithiocarbamate solution to train. absorption tube C. After 15 to 20 minutes, introduce 5 g of zinc granules into the conical flask A and quickly reassemble the apparatus. Allow the reaction to proceed for 45 to 60 minutes at room temperature. 5.2.2.2 Spectrophotomctric measurements - Disconnect the absorption .tube and tilt the absorber so that the reagent solution flows back and forth between the absorber and bulb to disperse the solid contents, if any, and to mix in the solution well. Transfer the solution to a photometric cell and measure its absorbance at the wavelength of maximum absorption, 540 nm, using water as reference liquid.
NOTE - The colour of the dispersion is not very stable for long time and hence absorptiometric ( nephplometric ) measurement should be made within 2 hours of the development of colour. Care should also be taken to prevent the evaporation of solution as its volume is small.

In the case of fritted glass absorber raise and lower the connecting tube into the absorber several times, to allow the solution to pass through the frit back and forth effecting the dispersal of the red deposit. Let the connecting tube finally drain into the absorber. 10 pg standard shall have an absorption 11 of the order of 0.4.

APPENDIX A ( CZauses0.4 and 5.1 )
PREPARATION A-l. PREPARATION OF OF TEST SOULTlONS OF ARSENIC SOLUTION under the

A-1.0 The preparation of test solutions may be considered three possibilities described in A-l.1 to A-1.3.

A-l.1 Sample Solution - A large portion of samples may be simply dissolved in water, \vith or without concentration, bromine treatment or addition of acid. A-l.2 Wet Oxidation - The organic matter is destroyed and arsenic compounds not directly reducible under conditions of test are broken down. Care shall be taken that fuming of the acid does not start until all the peroxide is used up for destruction of organic compounds. Generally, 50 percent ( z'/L~ ) hydrogen peroxide is used for destruction of organic compounds. 12

IS : 2088 - 1983 A-l.3 Solution of Difficult-to-Dissolve Substances of hydroperoxide

A-1.3.1 For opening up of siliceous materials; a mixture fluoric and sulphuric acid may be used but some hydrogen should be added before fuming of sulphuric acid starts.

A-1.3.2 Fusion with a mixture of sodium peroxide and sodium carbonate is useful in some cases where direct treatment with acids is not effective. If the sample is highly ferrogenous as in case of iron, ore, borax may be added in equal quantity.
